title: Seminar and Essay
tagline: Learn to read widely, think critically and then say something clear in writing and out loud.
overview: BC 4002 is a practical, skills-based course in which each student prepares a written essay (a short critical review) and presents a seminar on a topic in biochemistry and molecular biology. The topic is chosen with staff and varies by student, so this page focuses on the skills the course assesses: scoping a topic, searching and managing the literature, synthesising sources, structuring and writing an essay, citing correctly and ethically (including responsible use of AI tools), designing slides and delivering a talk. The units follow standard good practice for an honours-level seminar and essay.
whyItMatters: Scientists spend more of their working life reading, writing and presenting than pipetting. A clear review essay and a confident seminar are also the closest things in your degree to what graduate admissions panels, employers and examiners will ask you to do, and they teach you to think about evidence rather than memorise it.
studyTips: Start the reading list in week one and update it weekly; do not leave searching until the deadline.
Keep notes in your own words from the beginning to avoid accidental copying.
Write a messy first draft early; editing is easier than starting.
Practise the seminar aloud with friends who will ask questions.
Check the marking criteria and fit your essay and talk to them.

units.title: Choosing and Scoping a Seminar or Essay Topic
units.hook: A seminar topic that is too broad ('cancer metabolism') produces a lecture nobody can follow, and one that is too narrow leaves you with nothing to say. The craft lies in finding a question with enough literature to be answerable and enough tension to be interesting.
learningObjectives: Turn a broad interest into a focused question for a review-style essay or talk
Check that sufficient recent primary and review literature exists
Define the scope: what is in, what is out and why
Write a one-paragraph plan with a working thesis statement
Agree the plan with your supervisor or coordinator
Distinguish a descriptive summary from an argument

keyConcepts.definition: The boundaries of what the essay or seminar will cover, set so that it can be done well in the time and word limit.
A focused question that a literature review sets out to answer, such as 'How does X regulate Y, and what is uncertain?'
A one-sentence claim that your essay or talk argues for, rather than a topic label.
A critical overview of a topic that organises findings around themes or questions.
A question the literature has not yet answered or answers inconsistently.
Rules for deciding which papers belong in your review, for example date, organism or type of evidence.

deeper.beginner: Start with a topic you find interesting from a lecture, then ask three questions about it: what is known, what is disputed and what is new. A good seminar question usually has a 'how' or 'why' in it, and it is narrow enough that you can name five to ten central papers. Write your thesis statement as a sentence you could be asked to defend.
deeper.intermediate: Use a recent review to map the field and note its sub-topics. Pick a thread (a mechanism, a controversy, a technology) and test the question with a quick search to see how many primary papers exist from the past five to ten years. State the scope in writing: organism, time period, types of evidence. Discuss it with your coordinator before investing in reading.
deeper.advanced: Frame the essay as a contribution: synthesise findings to resolve or sharpen a controversy, compare competing models, or evaluate methods. Decide the organising principle (chronological, mechanistic, by model system, by evidence strength) and consider how that choice affects the conclusion. Be explicit about what the essay will not cover so that its omissions are principled.

commonMistakes: Choosing a topic as broad as a textbook chapter
Writing a descriptive tour of papers with no thesis
Relying only on a single review as the whole source base
Not checking whether recent primary literature exists

options: To state the central claim the essay argues for

units.title: Systematic Searching and Reference Management
units.hook: By the fifth essay you will have a thousand PDFs named 'paper(3).pdf' and no memory of which one said what. A reference manager and a repeatable search turn that pile into a library you can trust and cite correctly in minutes.
learningObjectives: Plan a search with synonyms, Boolean operators and appropriate databases
Use PubMed and Europe PMC filters to find reviews and recent primary papers
Capture references into Zotero (or a similar tool) with notes and tags
Generate in-text citations and a reference list in the required style
Check that every cited paper exists and says what you claim
Keep a log of your search

keyConcepts.definition: The planned combination of keywords, operators, filters and databases used to find sources.
Software that stores bibliographic details, PDFs and notes and formats citations automatically.
A set of rules (Vancouver, Harvard, APA, journal-specific) for how references appear in text and in the list.
A persistent identifier for a paper that resolves to its web location.
Finding more sources by following references in good papers and papers that cite them.
Reports, theses and preprints not formally published in journals; useful but needs careful judgement.

deeper.beginner: Pick two databases (PubMed and Europe PMC are free) and write the key concepts with synonyms before searching. Install Zotero and its browser connector, and save each paper you intend to use with one click. Add a note on why it matters when you save it, not later.
deeper.intermediate: Use filters for review articles and date ranges, then follow reference lists for primary papers. Tag items by essay section or theme and store notes in the reference manager. Use the word-processor plug-in to insert citations, choose the style your coordinator requires and check the output for errors such as missing DOIs or wrong author names. Record the date and query of each search.
deeper.advanced: Learn the limits of automatic metadata: check titles, years and journals against the source, and watch for retracted papers (reference managers can flag some). Consider shared libraries for group work and export backups regularly. Distinguish a citation to a paper you have read from a secondary citation, and cite the original when you can. Never cite a reference you have not located yourself, including any suggested by a text generator, because such tools can invent plausible-looking references.

commonMistakes: Citing a paper from its abstract alone without reading the methods or results
Typing references by hand and introducing errors
Copying a reference list from a review without checking the originals
Not backing up the reference library

options: It stores sources and formats citations consistently
It guarantees correct citations without checking
selfCheck.explanation: It saves time and reduces formatting errors, but you still need to verify the details.

options: Search PubMed or the publisher to confirm it exists and says what is claimed

selfCheck.explanation: Such tools can fabricate references, so every citation must be traced to a real paper that you have read.

selfCheck.question: What is snowballing?
options: Finding more sources through the reference lists and citing papers of key papers
selfCheck.explanation: Following references backwards and forwards is a quick way to find the core literature.

units.title: Reading and Synthesising Sources
units.hook: A weak essay is a series of paper summaries stapled together. A strong one asks what the papers say together: where they agree, where they conflict and why. That step is called synthesis, and it is where the thinking happens.
learningObjectives: Extract question, methods, result and limitation from each key paper efficiently
Organise notes in a matrix by theme rather than by paper
Identify agreements, contradictions and gaps across sources
Weigh evidence by design, sample size and consistency
Paraphrase accurately and attribute ideas
Draw a conclusion that follows from the evidence you assembled

keyConcepts.definition: Combining information from several sources to create a new understanding that no single source gives.
A table with papers as rows and themes or questions as columns, used to compare findings.
Re-expressing an idea in your own words and structure while still crediting the source.
A rough ranking of study designs by how well they control bias and chance.
Whether independent studies using different methods point in the same direction.
Systematically judging the quality and relevance of evidence.

deeper.beginner: For each paper, write four lines: the question, what was done, what was found and one limitation. Then lay the papers side by side under headings such as 'mechanism', 'model system' and 'conflicts'. If two papers disagree, ask whether they used different cells, doses or methods.
deeper.intermediate: Build an evidence matrix in a spreadsheet or table, with notes in your own words, and tag each cell with a page or figure reference. Group sources by sub-question and decide what the combined evidence supports, with what confidence. Mark where evidence is only correlative or only from one model system. Write your paragraph topic sentences from the matrix, not from individual papers.
deeper.advanced: Move from description to argument: propose a model that reconciles the conflicting results, or explain why the question remains unresolved. Consider confounders in comparing studies (different strains, assay sensitivity, endpoints), publication bias and the weight to give review claims that cite the same few original papers. Recognise when the best conclusion is a calibrated uncertainty, and say what experiment or data would resolve it.

commonMistakes: Writing one paragraph per paper with no comparison between them
Copying phrases from the abstract with a few words changed
Treating all evidence as equally strong
Ignoring a paper that contradicts your favoured view

selfCheck.question: What is the key difference between summarising and synthesising?
options: Synthesis combines sources to answer a question, while a summary reports each one separately
selfCheck.explanation: Synthesis creates a point that no single paper makes alone.

selfCheck.question: Two papers disagree. What is the first useful question?
options: Did they use different systems, doses or methods that could explain the difference?
selfCheck.explanation: Differences in conditions often explain conflicts and can become the interesting part of your essay.

selfCheck.question: Which is an acceptable way of using wording from a source?
options: Copy and change a few words
Understand it, restate in your own structure and cite it
Copy it without quotes but cite
Use it without citing since it is common
selfCheck.explanation: Genuine paraphrase plus citation respects both understanding and attribution.

units.title: Structuring a Scientific Essay or Review
units.hook: Readers decide in the first paragraph whether an essay is going somewhere. A clear structure, with an introduction that states the question and body sections that each carry one idea, is a kindness to your reader and a discipline for your own thinking.
learningObjectives: Plan a scientific essay with introduction, body and conclusion
Write topic sentences that state each paragraph's point
Use headings and transitions to guide the reader
Integrate figures, tables and mechanisms into the argument
Write a conclusion that answers the question and notes limits and future directions
Revise using a reverse outline

keyConcepts.definition: After drafting, list the main point of each paragraph to see whether the argument is logical and complete.
The first sentence of a paragraph, stating its main claim.
Words or sentences that connect ideas and show how one part leads to the next.
Telling the reader what is coming and why.
A diagram you draw yourself to explain a mechanism; copying published figures requires permission or a citation.
A short section on what remains unknown and what could be done next.

deeper.beginner: Begin with an outline: an introduction that gives context and your question, three or four body sections each answering part of the question, and a conclusion that states your answer. Write one claim per paragraph and support it with evidence from specific sources. Add a diagram of the central mechanism if it helps.
deeper.intermediate: Draft the body first, then write the introduction. After the first draft, make a reverse outline: if you cannot state the point of a paragraph in a sentence, rewrite or remove it. Check that the order of sections follows a logic (cause then effect, general then specific, controversy then resolution). Make figure legends self-contained and cite their sources.
deeper.advanced: Think about the argument's architecture: steelman opposing views before responding, calibrate claims to evidence, and make sure the conclusion does not introduce new claims. Balance breadth with depth by giving more space to the best-evidenced and most contested points. Edit for economy, since a review's value is in selection and judgement rather than the number of references.

commonMistakes: Starting with a long history of the field before reaching the question
Paragraphs that contain several unrelated points
Conclusions that only repeat the introduction
Reusing a published figure without citation or permission

selfCheck.question: What does a reverse outline reveal?
options: Whether each paragraph has a clear point and the argument flows
selfCheck.explanation: By listing each paragraph's main point you can spot gaps, repetition and weak ordering.

selfCheck.question: Where should the answer to the essay's question appear?
options: Clearly in the conclusion and prepared by the body
Nowhere; the reader should infer it
selfCheck.explanation: The conclusion should state the answer your evidence supports, with limitations.

selfCheck.question: Why draw your own mechanism diagram?
options: It shows your understanding and avoids copying issues
Because it is faster than writing
selfCheck.explanation: Drawing forces you to understand each step and avoids reproducing someone else's figure.

units.title: Clear Scientific Writing Style
units.hook: Good scientific prose is invisible: the reader sees the idea, not the sentence. That clarity is learnable, through short, concrete sentences, careful verbs and ruthless trimming of words that add nothing.
learningObjectives: Write concise, precise sentences with the key information first
Use consistent terminology and define abbreviations at first use
Choose verbs that match the strength of the evidence
Use numbers, units and symbols correctly
Edit for clarity and trim redundant words
Proofread for grammar, spelling and formatting

keyConcepts.definition: Wording that signals the strength of evidence, such as 'suggests', 'indicates' or 'demonstrates'.
Turning a verb into a noun ('the inhibition of' instead of 'inhibit'), which often makes sentences heavier.
Using one term for one concept so that the reader is not misled into thinking two things are different.
Standard scientific units with a space between value and unit (5 mM, 37 C), italics for gene symbols and correct case.
Choosing familiar words where they carry the meaning as well as technical ones.
A final pass for errors, best done on a printout or after a break.

deeper.beginner: Shorten any sentence that runs to three lines. Put the subject and the verb near the start and the new information at the end. Replace vague words ('a lot', 'very') with numbers or specific terms. Read your draft aloud: where you stumble, the reader will too.
deeper.intermediate: Match claim strength to evidence: say 'is required for' only if loss of the molecule blocks the process, and 'is associated with' if you only have correlation. Check consistency of abbreviations, units and gene/protein formatting. Cut empty phrases ('it is interesting to note that') and combine short choppy sentences when ideas are linked. Get a peer to mark where they got lost.
deeper.advanced: Study how strong papers structure paragraphs: old information first, new information at the end of a sentence, stress position for the main point. Be aware of discipline conventions, such as passive voice in methods, and of the pitfalls of non-native idioms and machine paraphrasing. When using editing or language tools, you remain responsible for accuracy and must follow disclosure rules.

commonMistakes: Using 'proves' when the data only 'suggest'
Switching between two names for the same protein in one essay
Leaving long strings of noun phrases that hide the action
Skipping proofreading because the deadline is close

selfCheck.explanation: A single correlational experiment supports association; causation needs stronger evidence.

selfCheck.question: Why use one term consistently for one concept?

selfCheck.question: What does a space between number and unit (5 mM) reflect?

units.title: Citation, Plagiarism and Responsible Use of AI
units.hook: You will rarely be tempted to copy a whole essay. The real risks are smaller: a sentence lifted from a review, an uncited idea, a reference you never opened. Understanding exactly where the line is makes you safer and a better scholar.
learningObjectives: Recognise forms of plagiarism including patchwriting and self-plagiarism
Cite sources for facts, ideas, data and figures in the correct style
Use quotation sparingly and appropriately in a science essay
Describe the main risks of using text-generating AI for essays
Follow your institution's policy on disclosure and permitted tools
Respond appropriately if you make a mistake

keyConcepts.definition: Presenting another person's words, ideas or data as your own without attribution.
Copying a source and changing a few words or the order, still too close to the original.
Reusing your own earlier submitted work without disclosure.
Facts that are widely known and undisputed need no citation, but when in doubt cite.
A citation produced by a text generator that looks real but does not exist or does not say what is claimed.
Software output showing text overlap with other sources; it needs human interpretation.

deeper.beginner: If an idea, number or sentence is not yours, cite where it came from. Write your notes in your own words so that you do not drift into copying. Use direct quotes rarely, in quotation marks, with a citation. If you are not sure whether something needs citing, cite it or ask.
deeper.intermediate: Understand your institution's plagiarism policy and the penalties. Keep your notes organised by source, so that you know whose idea is whose. Use the reference manager for consistent citation. Declare any permitted assistance, for example language editing, as policy asks. Treat AI output as untrusted: it may be wrong, may copy text, and cannot replace reading the papers.
deeper.advanced: Consider why attribution matters: it lets readers trace evidence, gives credit and protects you from repeating errors. Think about the ethics of authorship and the difference between permitted help (proofreading, discussion) and outsourcing the thinking that the assessment is designed to measure. Check the credibility of journals before citing from them and be cautious with predatory outlets.

commonMistakes: Believing that changing a few words makes copied text acceptable
Citing only at the end of a paragraph so that the source of each claim is unclear
Trusting an AI-generated reference list without checking
Reusing a previous assignment without permission

options: Quoting a sentence with quotation marks and a citation
Copying a paragraph and replacing a few words without citation
Citing a review for a general point
selfCheck.explanation: Changing a few words without attribution is patchwriting, which is still plagiarism.

options: Check that it exists and supports the claim before using it
Assume it is correct if the journal is real
selfCheck.explanation: Generated references can be fabricated. Only cite what you have found and read.

selfCheck.question: Why cite common-sense facts rarely but specific numbers always?
options: Specific data and claims need a traceable source, while universally known facts do not
selfCheck.explanation: Readers must be able to check data and contested claims.

units.title: Designing Slides and Visuals for a Seminar
units.hook: Slides are not the talk; you are. The best seminar slides do three things: orient the audience, show the evidence, and get out of the way so people listen to you.
learningObjectives: Plan the sequence of slides from a story outline
Limit text and use large, readable fonts
Create clear diagrams of mechanisms and pathways
Display data with simple, labelled figures
Cite sources on slides without clutter
Check the deck for accessibility and for timing

keyConcepts.definition: A sketch of the talk slide by slide before opening presentation software.
Each element should help the message; remove decorative or redundant items.
A simple labelled schematic that shows steps and arrows consistently.
Showing parts of a figure in steps so attention follows the explanation.
Readable contrast, colour-blind-safe colours and alt text where relevant.
Extra slides after the end for anticipated questions.

deeper.beginner: Write the title of each slide as the message (a sentence), then make the slide show it. Aim for roughly one slide per minute, with minimal text. Use one diagram at a time and point to each part as you talk. Use the same colour for the same thing throughout.
deeper.intermediate: Build pathway diagrams with consistent shapes and arrow styles, and use highlights to guide the eye. Enlarge data figures and label axes; show the comparison that matters. Put citations in small text at the bottom. Practise with the slides to check pace, and cut anything that you do not plan to talk about. Export a PDF as a backup.
deeper.advanced: Study how experienced speakers use visuals to carry complex relationships: build slides in layers, reduce cognitive load, and prepare analogies that you can mention explicitly as limited. Reconsider animations: they are useful only if they make a process clearer. Adapt the same content to a poster, a short talk and an extended seminar, changing the depth but not the message.

commonMistakes: Slides filled with paragraphs of text that the speaker reads
Tiny, unreadable axis labels
Different colours for the same protein on different slides
No time left for the conclusion

options: A sentence stating the slide's message

selfCheck.question: Why use consistent colours across slides?
options: It helps the audience track the same entity throughout
selfCheck.explanation: Stable visual coding reduces effort for the viewer.

units.title: Delivering the Seminar and Handling Questions
units.hook: Delivery is where nerves meet preparation. Most of what makes a speaker seem confident is rehearsal, a clear opening and the willingness to pause, and none of that is a talent you must be born with.
learningObjectives: Open the talk with context and a clear question
Manage time and pacing
Use voice, pauses and eye contact deliberately
Explain complex mechanisms step by step with the audience in mind
Respond calmly to questions and admit uncertainty honestly
Give and receive constructive peer feedback

keyConcepts.definition: An opening that tells the audience why the topic matters and how the talk is organised.
Spending time in proportion to importance, and practising to finish within the limit.
A deliberate silence that gives the audience time to absorb a point.
Repeating a question briefly so everyone hears it and you check you understood it.
Seminars often include chair-led discussion; answer to the room, not only to the questioner.
Specific observations on content, clarity and delivery to help the speaker improve.

deeper.beginner: Practise out loud at least three times, once to an audience, and time yourself. Open with one clear sentence on why the topic matters. Slow down at key points and pause. If a question is unclear, ask for clarification; if you do not know, say so and offer what you do know.
deeper.intermediate: Plan the first minute and last minute word for word. Create transitions between sections and rehearse them. Prepare answers to likely questions (what is the evidence, what are the limits, what next). During questions, listen to the end, restate, answer briefly and check that you answered. Give feedback to peers with one strength and one suggestion.
deeper.advanced: Treat delivery as communication design: adapt level and vocabulary to the audience, use analogies but state where they fail, and deal with hostile or off-topic questions by returning to evidence. After the talk, reflect on recordings or feedback and set one improvement goal for the next one. Think about how to present when you disagree with a prominent paper without being dismissive.

commonMistakes: Speaking too quickly because of nerves
Memorising a script and losing the place when interrupted
Answering a different question from the one asked
Running over time and skipping the conclusion
